newsitem.title: USA: Round-the-world balloonist on course over Atlantic.
newsitem.headline: Round-the-world balloonist on course over Atlantic.

text.p: American adventurer Steve Fossett was west of the Straits of Gibraltar on Thursday, happy and on course in his bid to circle the globe nonstop in a balloon.

At 7:30 a.m. EST (1230 GMT) his expedition headquarters in Chicago said Fossett's helium balloon had passed the Azores and was 700 miles (1,127 km) west of Gibraltar, expected to pass south of there in another 12 hours.

The expedition said the 52-year-old wealthy commodities broker was happy and the flight was trouble free, except for a lingering question of whether the Libyan government would grant permission to fly over that country.

Bo Kemper, chief spokesman for the record-setting solo attempt, said British Tycoon Richard Branson, whose own global balloon voyage failed a week ago, was attempting to intercede with the Libyan government on Fossett's behalf.

Permission has neither been given nor denied so far "and we have meteorologists trying to figure out how to go under or below (Libya)," Kemper said. "We have overflight permission from Niger, Chad and Sudan, Algeria and Morocco."

Fossett can alter his course by changing altitude to catch different winds. He has been drifting from 23,800 feet to 19,300 feet (7,254 to 5,883 metres). Kemper said he was roughly two days from Libya.

The balloonist lifted off from St. Louis late on Monday night in pursuit of one of manned flight's oldest goals but was forced to take a more southerly path than originally planned after he could not win permission from Russia to cross that country on a northern trans-European route.
The expedition said a number of minor problems, including language barriers affecting Fossett and flight controllers, made passage over Russia impossible.
After crossing North Africa he hoped to traverse Iran, Afghanistan, Pakistan, China, Mongolia, China again, perhaps Korea and then head out across the Pacific, the expedition said.
Kemper said Fossett was eating "meals ready to eat" -- prepared food used by the U.S. military -- and taking antacids to counteract their impact on his stomach.

He has been able to sleep periodically in his unpressurized, 6-1/2 feet long by four feet wide (two by 1.3 metres) yellow capsule, which is equipped with an alarm to rouse him should the balloon suddenly change altitude. The enclosed gondola is 5-1/2 feet high (1.7 metres).
The trip would take up to 18 days and the new route would not necessarily add to travel time, the expedition said.

His origial route was to have taken him from Britain over Western Europe, Russia, Kazakhstan and China. After crossing southern Japan he would have bridged the Pacific northeast to Washington state and land somewhere east of St. Louis. The trip may be followed on the Internet at the site http://www.luc.edu/solo.

The Colorado-based Fossett, who made a fortune in the Chicago futures markets, is financing the trip himself with scientific backing from Loyola University of Chicago, where his control centre is based. He made a similar attempt one year ago but crashed in Canada on the second day.

Two rival expeditions failed in the past week. A Swiss-Belgian team of Bertrand Piccard and Wim Verstraeten went down in the Mediterranean on Sunday six hours after taking off from the Swiss Alps, and Branson and two crew members brought their Virgin Global Challenger balloon down in Algeria a week ago less than 24 hours after taking off from Morocco.
